title: Write It Like a Pro
tagline: Voice and style · Writing for a reader · Revision
goal: Your kid picks a writing style (a review, a letter, a how-to, an opinion piece, a short story or a news report), picks a topic they actually care about, and writes something real for a real reader. Not a five-paragraph essay: a persuasive letter about bedtime, a how-to for their best skill. They learn that different situations call for different voices, and that writing for a real person changes how you put words together.
need: Paper and pencil, or a notes app
The Writing Style Cards near the end of this guide
A real reader: you, a grandparent, a friend

lesson.text: Every style does a different job, so the same topic sounds completely different depending on who's reading and why. Before writing a word, your kid answers two questions: who is this for, and what do they need from me?
lesson.before: Bedtime should be later because I want it to be.

model.line: Dear Mom, I'd like to propose a 9 p.m. bedtime on weekends. Here's my plan.
Bedtime at 8: two stars. Too early for summer, when it's still light out.
Local kid campaigns for later bedtime. Parents 'considering it.'
How to get a later bedtime: Step 1, show you can wake up on time.

lesson.modelNote: 'Because I want it to be' only convinces the writer. Each fix gives its reader what they need: Mom gets a plan, the review gives a reason, the news gives facts.

howTo.intro: Respond to what the words do to you: 'I got confused here' or 'this bit made me laugh' helps more than 'fix your comma.' Leave spelling for the final version.

plan.what: The style switch game, pick style and topic, think about the reader (Steps 1 and 2).
Write the first draft, then read it out loud for feedback (Steps 3 and 4).
Revise and send it to its real reader (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: They freeze at a blank page
troubleshoot.a: Say it out loud: 'Version 1 is supposed to be messy.' Then ask: what's the first thing you want your reader to know?
Normal. Ask them to give you feedback on something you wrote first. It shows them how it works.

steps.title: Play style switch
steps.why: A quick game that shows how much style matters, then the style and topic.
steps.kid: Pick something silly, like the family dog or last night's dinner. Your kid says one sentence about it as a news reporter, then as a restaurant critic, then as a letter to the dog. Then they flip through the Writing Style Cards, choose a style, and pick a topic they actually care about or know a lot about. They write it as one line: 'I'm writing a [style] about [topic].'
steps.you: Play the game too, the more dramatic the better. Then help them find a style and topic combination with enough to say, and let them choose.
ask: Which voice was the funniest, and why?
Who would actually want to read this?
steps.tip: A kid who's bored by the topic will write bored. Let them pick something they really care about.

levels.explore: Play one round, then pick a style and topic from the ideas.
levels.develop: Pick your own topic, and explain why your style fits it.
levels.extend: Pick two styles for the same topic, and predict how the pieces will differ.

steps.title: Know your reader
steps.why: Your kid figures out who they're writing for and what that person needs.
steps.kid: Before writing a word, your kid answers four questions: who exactly is reading this? What do they already know? What do they want: to be entertained, informed or convinced? And what tone fits: casual, formal, funny or serious?
steps.you: Ask the questions that make them think past themselves. A how-to for a five-year-old looks nothing like one for a teenager, and a letter to Grandma has a different tone than a letter to a company.
ask: If this person picked up your writing, what would make them keep reading?
Would you write this differently if your reader were five?
steps.tip: When kids know a real person will read it, they suddenly care whether it makes sense.

levels.explore: Name your reader and pick a tone.
levels.develop: Answer all four questions, and write one sentence about how your reader changes your writing.
levels.extend: Guess your reader's first 'but...', and plan your answer to it.

steps.title: Write the first draft
steps.why: The messy part: get the whole thing down, start to finish.
steps.kid: Your kid writes the whole piece in one go, using their style card as a loose guide. They keep going without stopping to fix spelling or rewrite sentences, and they say what they actually think. Bland and safe is worse than rough and honest.
steps.you: Protect the momentum: no corrections yet. If they get stuck, ask 'what's the next thing you want your reader to know?'
ask: What's the most important thing you want to say?
Are you writing what you think, or what you think sounds right?
steps.tip: Professional writers don't get it right the first time either. Saying that out loud helps more kids than you'd think.

levels.explore: Say it aloud, then write or dictate a few lines.
levels.develop: Write a full page with a clear opening, middle and ending.
levels.extend: Mark each sentence as opinion or evidence, and give every opinion at least one piece of evidence.

steps.title: Read it out loud for feedback
steps.why: Your kid hears their piece through a reader's ears.
steps.kid: Your kid reads the draft out loud to you or another family member and listens to the reaction. Then they write down 2 or 3 things to change: not everything, just what will make the biggest difference.
steps.you: Respond as a real audience, not a proofreader. Start with what works, then name one or two things that confused you: 'I got really interested when you talked about...', 'I got a little lost in the middle.'
ask: What part are you most proud of?
If you could change just one thing, what would it be?
steps.tip: If it sounds weird out loud, it reads weird on paper. Kids catch their own mistakes faster when they hear them.

levels.explore: Read it out loud and pick 1 thing to keep and 1 to change.
levels.develop: Write down 2 or 3 specific changes based on the feedback.
levels.extend: Have someone who doesn't know the topic read it, and fix what confused them.

steps.title: Revise and send it
steps.why: Version 2, then the piece goes to its real reader.
steps.kid: Your kid makes their changes: an opening that grabs, the main point clear early, no sentences that don't add anything, an ending that feels finished. They put Version 1 and Version 2 side by side and notice what changed. Then they send it to its real reader: mail the letter, test the how-to on someone, read the opinion piece at dinner.
steps.you: Help them see the gap between the two versions: that gap is the learning. Then help find a real (and safe) way to get it in front of someone.
ask: What's the biggest change between Version 1 and Version 2?
Who would enjoy reading this most?
steps.tip: If they don't want to share, ask why gently. Sometimes 'I don't want to' means 'I'm not sure it's good enough.'

levels.explore: Write a clean final version, circle one thing that's better, and share it with one person.
levels.develop: Rewrite the full piece with all edits, and send it to a real reader.
levels.extend: Cut it by a third, keep the main point, and send the shorter one.

reference.title: Writing Style Cards
reference.intro: Flip through these to choose a style. Each one says what the style does, how it's built, and what it sounds like.

lines.v: help someone decide if something is worth it.
what it is, what's good, what's not, who'd like it, your rating.
honest, specific, opinionated.
say something to one specific person.
greeting, why you're writing, the details, what you're asking, closing.
like you're talking to that person.
make your case so it's hard to ignore.
your opinion, best reason, second reason, the other side, what should change.
confident, direct, backed by facts.
bring an idea to life.
setting and character, a problem, what happens next, how it ends.
whatever fits the story: funny, spooky, quiet.
teach something so it actually works.
what you're teaching, what you need, numbered steps, tips.
friendly, clear, patient.
give the facts, fast.
headline, who/what/when/where first, details, a quote, what's next.
clear, factual, neutral. Short sentences.
teach or tell something people remember.
pick a tune everyone knows, keep the rhythm, write new lines that rhyme.
catchy, fun, packed with facts.

conclusion.headline: Version 2 went to the person it was written for.
conclusion.text: When there's a birthday card to sign or a note for a neighbour, watch what they do before the first word. You may see them stop and think about who's reading. And after feedback, see if they pick the change that matters most.
conclusion.celebrate: Point at the new opening in Version 2 and say: 'This one pulled me in. Read it to me again.'
extensions: Turn an informative piece into a song: keep a tune everyone knows, rewrite the lyrics
Write the same story twice, from two characters' points of view
Try every style card once over the next few weeks
Write the same topic in two styles and compare
Write a real letter to someone who'll write back
Keep a folder of finished pieces, one per style

signs: 'Who's this for?' comes up before they start writing
They write differently for Grandma than for a friend
They accept feedback and make the piece better
makeItReal: Send it off: mail the letter to a grandparent, send the complaint to the company, test the how-to on a friend. When a reply comes, read it together and decide what to write back.
cta: Want the next one? This guide is one of 120+ in the Anywhere Learning library, each with your job and your kid's job at every step.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

fromHome.text: In Panama City, my kids wrote the same made-up adventure twice: a treasure hunt in Santa Catalina, once from my son's point of view and once from my daughter's. They turned it into a book with pictures and recorded themselves reading it. In El Salvador, they each turned an informative text about the country into a song, set to a kids' tune we all knew.
